text: Agencies are working on the conditions that can be imposed like CCTVs, various other conditions, over and above what is applied to F&B outlets.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will also have to consult with the AGC, "Can we say no to an operator if we think it might be dodgy, even if the operators undertake to comply with the conditions?" It is not so straightforward.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Once these issues are assessed, the MTF has to decide on whether the opening or reopening can be allowed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now deal with the questions which have been raised on enforcement.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Assume we had said no to all pivoting of F&B operations, there would still be places which offer sex and meet-up opportunities; that was always going to happen.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we had one Police operation every single day on average since October 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To share a few examples, in October 2020, Police raided units along Ubi Road and Kallang Pudding Road, 57 persons were investigated for breach of SMMs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In November at Genting Lane, 24 persons were investigated for breach of SMMs, 10 women were arrested for work pass-related offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In February 2021 at Admiral Hill Road and, again, at Genting Lane, 88 persons investigated for breach of SMMs, one man arrested for working without a valid work permit.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In April, at Kitchener Road and Verdun Road, 45 persons investigated for breach of SMMs, seven men and one woman arrested.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In all the cases, items such as karaoke equipment, liquor, were seized; operators are being investigated.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Enforcement operations were also conducted over 20 weekends at every single festive occasion since October 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: About 400 F&B outlets including pivoted outlets were inspected in each operation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Since the onset of COVID-19, the rules are that hostessing is not allowed in any setting.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The women who were caught were likely in breach of their visit or work pass conditions and they were operating illegally.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the start of COVID-19 last year, we banned short-term visitors from coming into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, as of September last year, the ban on short-term visitors continued.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Basically, only Singaporean residents can come back, some of their relatives and some business travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In October last year, we introduced flexibility to allow boyfriends and girlfriends to come into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had almost a complete ban on short-term visitors, so boyfriends/girlfriends could not come in.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For background reference, between 2000 and 2019, there were about 120,000 Singapore Citizens who married non-residents.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: About one in four citizen marriages were between Singaporeans and non-resident partners.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is quite common for Singaporeans to have relationships with non-Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This boyfriend/girlfriend category was specifically introduced in the context of the ban on short-term visitors, to allow Singaporeans who were in relationships with foreign partners to be reunited because they had been separated for a long time due to border restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was after numerous appeals on this were received.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Meanwhile, there was a parallel development around September/October 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We announced Unilateral Opening to specific countries and regions which were of lower COVID-19 risk, including Vietnam, Brunei, New Zealand, Australia except Victoria state.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our assessment was the risk of importation of the virus was assessed to be low.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Vietnam, specifically, had a comprehensive public health surveillance system, had displayed successful control over COVID-19 at that time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the last four weeks of September 2020, it had zero local COVID-19 cases.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, under the Unilateral Opening, travellers could seek entry into Singapore by applying for an Air Travel Pass and this means short-term travellers from these countries were allowed to come in.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In February 2021, due to the worsening COVID-19 situation in Vietnam, we suspended the Unilateral Opening between Singapore and Vietnam, which meant that short-term travellers from Vietnam could not come in from February 2021 under the Unilateral Opening.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: ICA then began to receive many applications for Vietnamese to come into Singapore under the "boyfriend/girlfriend" category; people are quite inventive.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, to emphasise, once we suspended the Unilateral Opening with Vietnam in February 2021, there were many applications under the "boyfriend/girlfriend" category.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We looked at it, scratched our heads, the applications raised concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be one Vietnamese applicant and multiple sponsors claiming to be the lady's boyfriend.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be Singaporean sponsors, many who applied for multiple girlfriends.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But sponsors who are already married to someone else applying.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many men claiming to be a single lady's boyfriend, I mentioned it earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And sponsors who are unable to substantiate when we asked questions, "What relationship do you really have with this person who is proposed to become sponsored?" But as Members of Parliament will know, the residents will come to the Members of Parliament and say, "I am a Singapore Citizen, I have done National Service, why are you not allowing my girlfriend to come in?" We all have received such appeals.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You can no longer appeal for a boyfriend or girlfriend to come in.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In February, the Unilateral Opening with Vietnam was suspended.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The next month, in March, the "boyfriend/girlfriend" category was scrapped because we took the view that this was being abused.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We created this "boyfriend/girlfriend" category during a pandemic last year in October because we wanted to be compassionate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you wanted to rank the organisations in terms of compassion, I do not think most people will put ICA at number one on the list.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And MHA will not usually be accused of being the most compassionate either.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we did want to try and be compassionate and helpful because of the number of appeals and people want their loved ones to come in and we want to try and help.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But if the system is abused, then we have to stop it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If it is mutated, we have to stop it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, unfortunately, what that means is that many legitimate applications are now being refused.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They include MOM's Work Pass Holder Lane and MOE's Student's Pass Holder lane.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Applicants are required to submit their application to MOM and MOE respectively for entry approval and are subject to screening, obviously.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are also short-term visitors who were already in Singapore before the border controls were imposed in March 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For these persons, ICA assesses their application for extensions of their Short-Term Visit Pass on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It takes into consideration factors including restrictions on international travel, flight availability and whether the applicants have family ties in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Permanent Residents, unlikely to have committed any offence except for maybe safe distancing measures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Others on Work Pass would be in breach of their Work Pass conditions if they were performing services as hostess, but those on visit passes would be in breach as well by working without a Work Permit.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But if they say they were not working, then we have to show that they were in breach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, of course, the operators' operations, some of them are pivoted outlets, several of them are not, in other places, in warehouses and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We continuously have to look for them, rely on tip-offs as well as our own intelligence and keep trying to keep it under control.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few questions for Minister MTI, Mr Gan Kim Yong and originally, Minister for Health, but I think I will direct them to the Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first series of questions pertain to the differentiated regime between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals, which is part of the coming to terms and treating COVID-19 as endemic in the community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The query pertains to the negative pre-event tests that unvaccinated individuals will be required to undertake.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few days ago in Israel, the Prime Minister announced that the unvaccinated individual there will pay for the test.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not believe Minister clarified who pays for that test in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it would be helpful for the Minister to clarify that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question directed at Minister Gan pertains to supply issues of the vaccine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think, previously, in updates that the MTF had given, is this still a problem or are we on track to open the economy in concert with the plan that MTF has announced, by, I believe, it is September now?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The questions specifically on the KTV issues, indeed, as Minister Ong Ye Kung has mentioned earlier, lots of disappointment amongst Singaporeans, but I thought it would be important to have at least some understanding of common facts before coming to conclusions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the first question is with regard to the enforcement regime at the pivoted establishments, was it a heightened sort of enforcement regime?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But was there some specific attention paid on pivoted KTV establishments?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think earlier on, Minister Lawrence Wong spoke in a Facebook post about a cat and mouse game.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Were additional conditions imposed on certain operators in view of their past record or reputation, so to speak?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in this regard, again, was there a differentiated regime from the enforcement agencies to pay more attention to some of these establishments?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, finally, I have received some emails from members of the public about warnings that they have given the authorities about some of these KTV establishments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many warnings or pieces of feedback did – not just MHA but also MOH and the other agencies – receive on egregious SMM violations in KTV establishments?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is still on track and the key is to look at the progress in our vaccination programme, which, as Minister for Health has explained just now, is picking up momentum.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But it is important for us to focus a lot more on the vaccination of our senior population which is of a greater concern to all of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: If we do have many serious cases, we will have a problem with the capacity of our healthcare system which will then result in a higher mortality rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we need to continue to keep an eye on our number of serious cases and at the same time, make sure that our vaccination rate is high.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Then, we will be able to progressively, step-by-step, reopen our economy or open up our borders to allow for travel in and out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And as I have mentioned in my speech, these details are still being worked out and we will share more details later on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I will ask Minister Lawrence Wong to talk about testing because this relates to the national policy on testing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The question, I believe, was about who pays for the cost of tests, if the person is unvaccinated, to get into a venue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The thinking is that the rule is that for certain activities, certain settings, we will require vaccinated persons only.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And from the Government's side, the rule will be that if the person is not vaccinated, not fully vaccinated, then he will have to produce a confirmed negative test.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will let venue operators and owners decide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They may want to set up an operation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A restaurant might want to do that; a venue operator might want to do that; a MICE event organiser might want to do that, because it says, "Look, I want to do that to let unvaccinated persons come in." If not, then, he may well say, "Look, it is up to the individual.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The individual has to go to the clinic, get a test and then show me the result." So, the Government sets the rule, the framework.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Individual organisations that are looking at the framework can then decide whether or not they want to provide the test for their customers, or if they will require their customers to get the test from a clinic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I noted, I think there were four questions, if I got it right, from Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is quite apart from what Safe Distancing Ambassadors and so on do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, I think Mr Singh wanted to know if there was a particular focus on pivoted outlets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, there were a number who were not to be operating at all and, in fact, totally illegal operations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I would say, in terms of seriousness, those are particularly pernicious, in terms of transmission, the kind of activities and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And nothing is supposed to be happening in a warehouse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, those kinds of operations were busted as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, a broad range and also F&B operations which were not pivoted operations, just simply reopening.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also, some of them had been in breach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do not mistake me to think that every single one was, therefore, engaging in what we might consider to be shady activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we needed to target a broad range.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume Mr Singh is not asking for the closing down of every operation as long as there is any breach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Depending on the nature of the breach, there will be a penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, got egregious breaches, there will be closure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I would not ascribe to Mr Singh the suggestion that Police now should get even tougher and just close everyone down as long as there is one breach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The last point I think was whether warnings given by the public were taken seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not do the operations obviously, but I think most Members will know how, in general, the Police intel system is expected to work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police have their own intelligence framework, their own ground framework and public tip-offs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of crimes are solved by public tip-offs and they are important, they are taken seriously and I assume that goes into the assessment framework on what operations to conduct.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a last question by Mr Pritam Singh on vaccine supplies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Supplies continue to be in shortage throughout the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many developing countries are still trying to secure supplies and, in the earlier stage of the pandemic, we, too, were short of supplies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, fortunately, we had negotiated advance purchase agreements (APAs) with major suppliers in the early stage of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As time goes on, the testing system will also evolve.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, in time to come, if you have gotten a negative test result, you may be able to attend multiple events and multiple premises.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is not just one event to one test.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we just have to bear that in mind.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first is stemming from a worry about discrimination on treatment between those who have been vaccinated versus those who are unable to and those who do not wish to be vaccinated and the treatment that they receive.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the one hand, I empathise and hear the calls of those saying, "What is the point of being vaccinated if I am still faced with certain restrictions or why are we being penalised?" But at the same time, I know full well the impact of some of those who are unvaccinated for various medical reasons, in particular, our seniors and the social impact of the isolation not being able to be involved in activities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I wonder if, in the TraceTogether app, for example, we might consider amending it to show those who are vaccinated, those who are not vaccinated and those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons and if there can be differentiation of treatment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And also, how this might take into account, for example, families who have seniors or children who are unable to be vaccinated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving to my second group of clarification points, I think we have spoken about the KTV cluster.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I would also like to ask about the Jurong Fishery Port cluster as this spread has impacted stallholders, workers and residents alike in both my Cheng San and Chong Boon markets as well as food centres.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Minister please elaborate what led to the spread of COVID-19 in the Jurong Fishery Port, whether there are clearer findings on the mechanism of transmission of COVID-19 into the Port and subsequently into our local markets and whether our seafood is safe for consumption?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do our SMMs need changing and how can we ensure the safe reopening of Jurong Fishery Port and our markets and hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The differentiation helps protect those who are not vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member asked about whether TraceTogether app can indicate vaccination status.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second is that children or seniors who, because of medical conditions, are not allowed to be vaccinated, whether they get left out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Earlier on, when we came out with the "two-five rule", one of the criticisms is that it was so confusing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And indeed, the confusion arises because of the exemptions we were trying to give.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, in a group of five, all vaccinated, but you allow up to two children below 12 who cannot get vaccinated, but can join part of the group.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are negative, you can join the group.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is something we will consider as we do our mid-term review.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Lastly, I do want to reiterate a point I made earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By then, there will probably be justification for lesser differentiation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the point on whether seafood is safe, seafood is absolutely safe to consume.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How did the virus get into the Jurong Fishery Port?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to see if we can trace the sources of the infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as of now, it does not help us to suppress the cluster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It helps us understand the infections, the infiltration, how it happened and it helps us strengthen the safe management measures in future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Because of the important impact that the cluster has on this topic, I think it is important for us to give the House an account on the Jurong Fishery Port (JFP) as well as our food supply and its impact on hawker centres and markets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, with your permission, Deputy Speaker, may I address some of the Parliamentary Questions (PQs) that Members have filed on a related subject as well?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members Mr Dennis Tan12,13,14 and Ms Nadia Samdin have filed PQs on the same subject set down for a later Sitting.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Several Members have also filed related PQs for a later Sitting, which I will address together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members Yip Hon Weng15 and Mr Dennis Tan on measures taken to mitigate the transmission of COVID-19 at our fishery port and key food facilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Dennis Tan on assistance given to the companies and workers at JFP, Mr Darryl David16 on support given to stallholders at markets and hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have worked closely with industry partners over the years to build diversified food supply chains.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The remaining two-thirds of our seafood imports are distributed to the industry via other routes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it is a very diversified distribution platform.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Following the closure of JFP on 17 July, Singaporeans were understandably worried.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some had rushed to buy seafood over that weekend.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We saw an increase in footfall at supermarkets, after the market seafood stallholders were required to get tested on 18 July.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They could open their stalls only after receiving a negative PCR swab test result.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: All JFP workers were quarantined, thus affecting the operations of many suppliers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Phase Two (Heightened Alert) restrictions on dining in moderated the demand.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Singapore Food Agency (SFA) and Enterprise Singapore (ESG) responded quickly to facilitate distributors and supermarkets to activate alternative arrangements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These arrangements include diverting supplies directly to the supermarkets' distribution centres and retail outlets.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Supermarkets themselves increased their stock of fresh produce through their suppliers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They have been keeping their retail shelves well-stocked with a variety of seafood including the frozen seafood varieties.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As the market seafood stalls resumed operations, some switched to SFP for their supply or sourced from alternative suppliers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I visited the Jurong Cold Store last Wednesday which stocks supplies of frozen shrimp, sea bass and grouper among others.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The cold store facility serves many wholesalers, supplying to the supermarkets and food establishments islandwide.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the same time, retail food establishments are adjusting by switching to frozen alternatives.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our local farms also produce a good variety of seafood such as sea bass, tilapia and grouper and some of them have reported many-fold increase in inquiry and orders.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And they can be found online, for example, on Lazada's RedMart, FairPrice online shop and at the supermarkets as well, such as Prime and FairPrice.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I encourage Singaporeans to broaden their choices of seafood and where they buy their seafood from.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have been reviewing the longer-term plans for this sector.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Since 2020, SFA has been conducting studies on the enhancement of the wholesale fresh produce sector and it is working with NEA to study the wet market sector to better meet the future demands of consumers and industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will factor in lessons learnt from this episode to better future-proof the sector.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This episode has truly tested the resilience of our supply chains.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our overall seafood supply situation has remained stable because of our diversified supply and distribution channels.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA and ESG will work with industry partners to strengthen their business continuity plans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And I would also like to thank all the industry players for stepping up in this period of crisis.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our fishery ports, Pasir Panjang Wholesale Centre (PPWC), abattoir and slaughterhouses are key nodes in our food supply chain.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA has begun working with the companies operating in these facilities to implement Safe Management Measures (SMMs) since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our objectives are to protect public health by minimising the spread of the virus and to ensure business continuity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To minimise risk of infection from foreigners, contactless delivery for the truck drivers and boatmen was implemented.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Controlled access to these facilities has been in place with only workers and registered trade visitors allowed to enter.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, public can no longer go there for a "look-see, look-see".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Workers at these facilities have been encouraged to get vaccinated quickly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Unfortunately, COVID-19 managed to breakthrough these defences, with many cases detected at JFP over the past month.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The cases further spread to the markets and hawker centres through the stallholders who had visited JFP.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Investigations by MOH and SFA are ongoing to determine how transmission had taken place in JFP and we have all heard from Minister for Health earlier on.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, the humid and laborious environment made it uncomfortable for workers to wear their masks for prolonged periods of time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This meant a higher propensity for workers to adjust their masks or take them off momentarily.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, the workers could have taken off their masks while they take their breaks, smoking breaks, for example, and socialise in close proximity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, JFP, being a marketplace, meant that the workers and traders mix freely throughout the facility.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is just like the market that we are used to, shoppers going around, traders going around and sometimes, between stallholders they mix as well as they move stocks from one to another.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some contactless delivery measures were not strictly followed.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will address these areas in our SMMs, with practical solutions and enforcement before we re-open JFP.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The first round of deep cleaning of JFP was done on 18 July and we will be conducting another round before it is re-opened.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Common areas and crates will be regularly cleaned during its operation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Contactless delivery protocols for truck drivers and boat men will be stepped up.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Trade visitors who are not on any COVID-19 testing regimes, such as RRT will be subjected to an Antigen Rapid Test (ART) before entering.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: More frequent patrols will be carried out to ensure compliance with the SMMs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are working closely with MOH and when informed of their epidemiological investigation, we will adjust these enhanced measures if necessary, to better protect both the workers and trade visitors.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA has audited the SMMs at SFP and PPWC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It will progressively cover all the other key food facilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One-time PCR swab test of all workers is being carried out.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I am very glad to report that we are not seeing big clusters in these facilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Seven-day RRT and enhanced SMMs will be rolled out to these facilities as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will monitor the operation closely and take enforcement action for any non-compliance with SMMs at these facilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: An alternative site is being made available for use in the event of another closure of the fishery ports or PPWC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Collective responsibility is required to keep everyone safe.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Next, on assistance extended to JFP and related businesses.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The relevant agencies are working with companies to provide the necessary assistance during this difficult period.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have been facilitating companies to redirect supplies directly to the supermarkets' distribution centres and retail outlets so that they can continue operations despite the closure of JFP.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are also coordinating closely with the companies to ensure that their workers have been swabbed and are healthy before we resume operations at JFP next week.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Eligible workers and self-employed persons can apply for the COVID-19 Recovery Grant-Temporary.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Those under quarantine can also apply to MOH for financial assistance under the Quarantine Order Allowance Scheme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And as to the support for stallholders in markets and hawker centres, the Government is committed to supporting our hawkers and working with them through this difficult period.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The money will be directly credited into the bank accounts of the stallholders.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is on top of a third month of rental waiver and subsidies for fees for table cleaning and dish washing services provided this year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Those under quarantine can apply for the Quarantine Order Allowance Scheme and those eligible may apply for the COVID-19 Recovery Grant COVID-19 Recovery Grant-Temporary.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For hawkers that continue to face financial issues, they can also approach NEA, who will review their case and provide case-by-case support.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: On Ms Nadia Samdin's question about measures to improve safety at our markets and hawker centres, NEA will be putting in place tightened SMMs at all markets and hawker centres to ensure that they remain clean and safe for stallholders and patrons, bearing in mind that many of our hawker centres and markets are frequented by elderly patrons.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will facilitate the testing, such as setting up more quick testing centres, as announced by MOH and explore teaching hawkers to conduct self-testing at steady state.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mandatory SafeEntry check-in will be implemented at all markets and hawker centres managed by NEA or NEA-appointed operators to facilitate more effective contact tracing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We had previously introduced e-payments to go cashless and will encourage hawkers and patrons to use this mode of payment to minimise contact and also possibility of fomite transmission.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it is a very high vaccination rate, 90%.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And we are calling up, encouraging those who have yet to do so to go for vaccination as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While we will continue to ensure the cleanliness of our hawker centres through regular cleaning and disinfection, I also want to remind all patrons to adhere to SMMs and to observe personal hygiene.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: By way of clarification, I would like to raise three questions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A number of Clementi residents feel very much affected by the recent outbreak.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many worried parents, seniors, families are concerned about the way forward.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The first question is relating to the Jurong Fishery Port cluster.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Three weeks ago, I filed a Parliamentary Question on detecting COVID-19 virus in the built environment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the task force what efforts are being made to look for other areas and workplaces that could be potential hotspots but which have not yet come to surface, but which are still at higher risk?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A number of parents in Clementi have been watching the reports of some schools having students infected, possibly by transmission at home and they want to know, given the Delta variant, what measures are being taken to maintain the safety of students, especially younger children, who are not yet able to be vaccinated?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, how soon can we roll out breathalysers and tests, which are easy enough for a child to do it themselves?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Third question, Sir, even as we open up and transition, I ask the Ministries that we must maintain many of the capabilities built up during this pandemic and internalise the lessons learnt because we know that a worse variant of COVID-19 or even a future Disease X, a worse pandemic, is just a question of "when" rather than "if".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I thank the Ministers and our public servants for their efforts and I seek these questions as clarification.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say there are three broad criteria.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That includes our airport, our seaports, the different interfaces with the external environment and, there, we want to put in greater precautions, safeguards, including regular testing, for the people who are working there.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thirdly, it is an assessment of areas where we think SMMs may not be effectively done.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we look around and there is a qualitative assessment, our SDAs are out there, enforcement officers are out there and if we see that, potentially, in this particular industry, in this particular work site, SMMs are not followed, then that raises the alarm bells and we will want to take a closer look at that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this is constantly being done and we are always looking at potential areas of risk where we would want to put more attention or require more testing to be done.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On schools, that is also something we are watching carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think the school protocols have, fortunately, been very tight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We hope that can continue and that is, in part, because our schools have been very stringent in keeping and complying with these protocols.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But still, beyond just having safe management measures, we would certainly look at putting in place a testing regime, especially when there are more convenient methods of testing which can be scaled up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We just have to continue this process of building better capabilities to protect ourselves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am asking this question on behalf of some seniors who have conveyed to me their frustration that while they are being urged to get vaccinated, they are unable to get an appointment for a Sinovac vaccination.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think we do have a group of individuals who prefer vaccinations using the traditional approach and have reservations about newer technologies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, given that we are especially concerned about vaccination for our seniors, what avenues are there available for these seniors who prefer the traditional approach?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there plans to further expand the Sinovac vaccination?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think, first of all, is to try to explain to the seniors, which I have tried a lot, which is that the mRNA vaccine actually has been developed for many, many years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not something so novel and so new.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It went through all the rigorous evaluation by different authorities and then approved and, so far, even in Singapore, a few million people have taken it, around the world even more and it is proven to be safe and effective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every vaccine will have side effects, including Sinovac, including mRNA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is a good vaccine and, as far as possible, we want to persuade everyone, including our seniors, to take the mRNA vaccine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But for those who are simply not comfortable or they are contra-indicated for mRNA vaccine and they want to take the Sinovac vaccine, we now have made it available under the Special Access Route.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the great majority of Singaporean seniors actually still prefer the mRNA vaccine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You have got to wait a while, but you eventually will get the vaccine.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Sorry, Minister, I should clarify that they actually tried to make the appointment but they are told that it is fully booked.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you can give me the contact, we will be more than happy to help them facilitate and make an appointment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are 20 over clinics that are doing that now.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They asked why the F&B sector seems to be bearing the brunt of each of the heightened measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Minister why did we reverse on the 19 July decision to have fully vaccinated five-person dine-n?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It appears to be a reasonable proposition where the diners among them are fully vaccinated and this is, indeed, the kind of scenario we are looking at.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And with that kind of de-risking, why do we not allow that to continue?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I thought I spent half an hour explaining why we need to revert to Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, the risk profile was significantly different from when we first started planning for the "two-five rule" framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we had to make a very painful decision.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I must share with you that we deliberated at length on this issue.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We fully appreciate the challenges the F&B sector is facing and is still facing today until we are able to restore dining-in.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have been working with MOF to roll out support packages to help them tide over this difficult and challenging phase, and the Minister for Finance and I met them and tried to understand their concerns and to also reassure them that we are aware of their challenges and we will do what we can to help and support them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I must also say that the reason that they usually face the brunt of our measures is because as Minister Wong pointed out earlier, they are front-facing.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And there is a lot of interaction in restaurants and F&B outlets.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, it is one of the very high-risk settings and we have to be extra careful and exercise additional caution.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Unfortunately, when we have to tighten our measures to protect the community, we will need the F&B sector to work with us.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The exact mechanism for transmission is unclear up to now.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Were these foreign fishermen required to take any COVID-19 tests or be vaccinated before entering the fishery port?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If not, can this be introduced immediately to prevent further import of the virus where the countries where the pandemic is raging?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, regarding the Sinovac vaccine, is the relatively lower efficacy rate of the Sinovac vaccine, compared to the mRNA vaccines, the reason why those who got the Sinovac vaccine are not considered fully vaccinated in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This lower efficacy rate has been known for some time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why did MOH not make this known clearer that they will not be giving the same recognition to the Sinovac vaccine as the mRNA vaccines yet, for the purpose of differentiated measures?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because this could have blunted the demand for the vaccine, which was mentioned earlier, and convinced more people to get the mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, as we reopen our borders, many more foreigners will be entering Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there plans to require vaccinations for both short- and long-term visitors so that they do not inadvertently reduce our overall vaccination rate?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, a recent British study found that a longer period of eight weeks between vaccinations produces a higher immune response than a spacing of three weeks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In our haste to get people fully vaccinated, where we are encouraging people to book their second dose three weeks after the first dose, will we be compromising on maximising durable immunity to COVID-19 in the longer term?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Indeed, I think that there is a hypothesis that the cluster may have come through or punched through a fisherman on a fishery boat.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: That hypothesis actually has not been confirmed at this point in time, but we are not waiting for that.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: That is along with the strengthened, heightened SMMs at the PPWC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have instituted that also for Senoko and Jurong Fishery Ports.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But with regard to the question about whether we should subject them to vaccinations or Antigen Rapid Tests (ARTs), that is something that we are considering at this point in time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Whatever we do, I think we are looking for practical solutions where we can do it without increasing the risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We actually do not allow them to land on our shore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If we subject them to frequent tests, that may be a way for them to actually be landing more frequently on our shore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we have to evaluate these options and look for practical and effective solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is recorded that you are vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the question is whether it should then be conferred the concessions, should we have differentiated safe management measures?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would say that, currently, there are different vaccines and every vaccine has a different efficacy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From a public health point of view, it would not make sense to just treat every vaccine the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned in my Statement just now that the efficacy of the Sinovac vaccine against the Delta variant, because of the places that it has been applied and administered, that data is still being built up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that data has now been submitted, early this month.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we have a lot of data now before us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The data on efficacy against the Delta variant is building up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will assess them robustly and if it is approved under PSAR, naturally, it will be recognised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The third question, if I get correctly, is if we allow travel lanes to open, whether we will ensure that travellers to Singapore are also vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As explained by Minister Lawrence Wong just now, I think we have to open up travel very carefully, step by step.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If not, you will inject infections into our community and make things go out of control again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, for example, we have unilateral opening for very safe regions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So far, it has not caused community spreading because we assessed those regions and know that they are very safe.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think whatever step we take, we must always make sure that it does not raise our risk level but maintain or even lower our risk level.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I welcome the MTF's focus on future differentiated treatment for the vaccinated and unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is perhaps one of the tools in the kit to persuade and encourage, nudge and cajole those who are still considering.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I wish to return to a suggestion I made at the very beginning of the national vaccination programme, which is to consider making vaccinations mandatory.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A lot of effort has gone into encouraging Singaporeans to be vaccinated because it makes sense.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore considered it our civic duty to be vaccinated if there are no medical grounds to refuse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, the fear is that the freedom of a minority to choose not to be vaccinated will affect the freedom of the majority who have chosen to be vaccinated for the sake of themselves, their families and the community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second clarification I seek is with regard to the effectiveness of TraceTogether and SafeEntry for contact tracing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the last few days, with regards to the KTV cluster and also partially to the Jurong Fishery Port cluster, we heard some limitations vis-à-vis contact tracing because people who do not bring their phones with them or their dongles with them because of fear of being detected in certain places.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, whether or not the MTF can comment on whether contact tracing has been made more difficult recently.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, on differentiated treatment, I quote a comment that was made by fellow Member Nadia Samdin on differentiated treatment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I welcome it, how will we eventually distinguish between those who knowingly avoid vaccination and those who do not have a choice, for example, the young and the medically excused?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is, of course, if we do not introduce mandatory vaccination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I did not quite get the second question so maybe Minister Lawrence Wong can help answer that later.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because as of now, the use of the vaccine is under PSAR, the Pandemic Special Access Route.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is under emergency use, in a pandemic situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To make it mandatory, I think is not quite consistent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In time to come, when COVID-19 is really endemic, maybe it is a policy that governments around the world will have to consider.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the third question, which is related to Ms Nadia Samdin's question, how do we distinguish between those who knowingly choose not to vaccinate versus those who cannot get vaccinated?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From a public health point of view, they are actually the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are equally vulnerable and we ought to treat them the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are not vaccinated, to protect you, best not to join the big events.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It cannot be that because your intention is different, we let you join.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That would not make sense from a public health point of view.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, as I mentioned earlier, we will think of measures, such as you get yourself tested and you can join or, in time to come, when our vaccination rate is very high and our collective resilience is so strong, we actually do not need much of that differentiation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second question is on contact tracing, the effectiveness of TraceTogether and SafeEntry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say generally, even in the recent episode, we have seen that the systems are in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Most people, the vast majority, are using the TraceTogether tokens or the app properly; establishments are having proper gating and check-ins using SafeEntry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so overall, we still find this to be very effective in doing timely contact tracing and ringfencing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Are there people who abuse this, who do not use the TraceTogether app?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But by and large, it has still been very effective and we want to make it even more effective, which is why for markets and hawker centres, previously, we had not put SafeEntry check-in requirements for all markets and hawker centres; because we all know it is very difficult.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: People come in from all the different places.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will lead to some inconveniences on the ground with many of your residents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I seek Members' understanding to explain to your residents why this is necessary in order for us to have effective contact tracing during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sorry, Mr Deputy Speaker, I missed out one question by Mr Gerald Giam just now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He mentioned whether we are rushing dose one and dose two by keeping only a three-week duration and whether a longer duration will make the vaccine more effective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is the hypothesis of one study and it is not conclusive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are many other studies that show that three weeks for the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine and four weeks for the Moderna vaccine is an appropriate duration and delivered good efficacy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think the conclusion is not definite.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And the easy way to do it, either you buy a self-test kit from the pharmacy or you walk into one of these quick test centres, do a self-swab or do a breathalyser test.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And, under those circumstance, I think we need to study the demand pattern and, if need be, we will need to operate on more days of the week or for longer hours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as we move into the next phase and, judging by the demand, we will have to adjust the timing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Earlier on, Minister Ong Ye Kung had noted that the vaccination rate was progressing at an impressive 1% per day and that we could expect a 70% coverage by around mid-August and, possibly, 80% by September.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am wondering what the basis for such an optimistic projection is, in part because once we factor in the under-12 in the population, for instance, that would not qualify for vaccination, you get something in the order of 10%-12%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, it only assumes an 8%-9% vaccine hesitancy share of the population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Elsewhere, it has been demonstrated that at far lower coverage rates, populations have seen a point of inflection where there is resistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I guess the question is: how would we get this coverage to this 80% that, I agree, would certainly be welcomed?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The basis of projection is because we watch the number every day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is right that, if that comes about, that means vaccine hesitancy in Singapore is actually much lower, compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think this is a function of us working together as a united people, trusting each other, with trust between Government and people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that is what helped us overcome vaccine hesitancy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We still have a lot of work to do for those who are older, but let us continue this work.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think when the task force announced that we are going to release the Sinovac vaccine to the people, many rejoiced, they were very happy about it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But this rejoicing was short-lived after it was announced that the Sinovac vaccine – once you are vaccinated – is not considered as part of the national vaccination programme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I also understand that there are overseas Singaporeans who are vaccinated with AstraZeneca or other vaccines and I think MOH is prepared to accept them if they do a serology test.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And if the serology test shows that they have immunity, they can be included in the national registry.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My question is: for Singaporeans who have received the Sinovac vaccine, if they are willing to go through a serology test and the serology test shows that their immunity is there, can you register them in the national registry?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, when next month or the month after next, when the restrictions are lifted for the vaccinated, can they be considered as part of the vaccinated instead?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Second clarification is on the supply of vaccines.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am very happy to hear that there is enough vaccine for all of us and, by September, we probably will hit about 80%.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I read in the papers, our neighbour, Johor Bahru, has about 15% vaccination as of last month and I think Batam's was 23%.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My question is: can Singapore help our immediate neighbours with their vaccination once we have hit our 80% because, if our neighbours are not safe, we are not safe as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the issue of the Sinovac vaccine, I have explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Rather than doing serology tests – and amongst our experts, there are also different interpretations of serology tests – I think the easiest thing is to go back to what I have said just now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is trying to do it as fast as it can.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if the Sinovac vaccine or other vaccines in time get approved under PSAR, naturally, we will want to take a more inclusive approach in recognising them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our contracts require us to discuss with the suppliers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, certainly, where we can help, we will want to help our immediate region because it is only when every country around the world and in the region recovers from COVID-19 that we will really be able to live with COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The clarification I would like to seek pertains to the longer term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, beyond immediate easing and reopening, when we are well and truly into a new normal of endemic COVID-19; in this new normal, as Minister Ong Ye Kung has noted, we will have reached a high level of vaccination and, therefore, COVID-19 resilience in the population and the need for differentiation between vaccinated and unvaccinated persons would be less.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But Minister Lawrence Wong has also said that, as we reopen, we must expect the case numbers to rise.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, to take this a little bit further, in the new normal, there is still a possibility that we get a major flare-up in infections from time to time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in such a scenario, the few hundreds of thousands or half a million persons or so who remain unvaccinated will be the ones at greatest risk of severe illness and therefore, at greatest risk of loading our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, in such a scenario, I would like to ask the MTF how might we tame the flare-up and would the MTF then consider in such a scenario a sharper differentiation, albeit a transient or interim one in SMMs between vaccinated and unvaccinated persons so that we can protect the unvaccinated but yet not cause a major disruption to normal life for the vast majority like we now have in Phase Two (Heightened Alert)?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And more to the point, do we think we still need to pull back – to use Minister Lawrence Wong's words – pull back sharply as a population from time to time in the new normal or can we finally expect to see the last of Phase Two (Heightened Alert)?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Xie would like clarity in the months forward.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Maybe in September and beyond that, we will consider sequential moves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But each time we do so, we do it step-by-step and we do it in a controlled manner, not a big bang.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And whenever we make one move to ease, we monitor health outcomes very closely, precisely for the concerns that Mr Xie has highlighted, that there will still be unvaccinated persons and we are concerned that when we make one step to open, cases go up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have to watch the health outcomes and the hospitalisation and ICU cases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The worst case in my mind would be when a new variant strikes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: No one knows exactly when this will happen and what what sort of new variants we will see.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if a new variant emerges down the road that is much more transmissible or worse, lethal and more resistant to the current batch of vaccines, then it is almost like you are dealing with a new virus frankly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Therefore, the defences have all got to go up again.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, while we are embarking on this journey of reopening, let us understand that there are still risks, there are still uncertainties ahead and, therefore, we are taking this controlled step forward, remain alert, remain vigilant and continue to be flexible and adaptable in adjusting our posture, based on the latest assessment of risks and the external environment and how the pandemic proceeds.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I will take two more clarifications before closing the debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just one clarification for the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There will be some individuals who have both doses and who still have very low resistance to the virus due to them being immuno-compromised for genetic reasons or to reasons due to having certain risk factors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is the Government actively looking at – and this can relate to the Parliamentary Question that I have filed – is the Government actively looking at giving a third jab to such individuals if the science actually supports that that will help them to raise their resistance to the vaccine?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I understand that the US Centres for Disease Control is actively looking at this question right now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when the Expert Committee has made a decision, we will make the information public.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Just a change to direct my question to Minister Shanmugam.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I had earlier filed a Parliamentary Question for a later Sitting but I thank the Minister for answering it earlier.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I know the Minister had addressed this in quite some detail but I am just wondering how will the surveillance and enforcement be stepped up further, given the current possibility and especially in areas, such as industrial spaces, where perhaps office or factory spaces could be used for parties at night, based on some anecdotal feedback that we have heard?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we have to rightly focus on the people who are the cause of the spread, people who operate illegally and the people who patronise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, before the pandemic, what was our framework?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you need to be realistic about what is doable and what is not doable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we allowed the nightlife outlets, pubs, bars, KTVs, those who wanted to pivot, what was our understanding of the situation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But does that mean that, immediately, all dodgy activities would have stopped?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The issue is that there is money to be made in making available the services and there will always be people, because there is a huge demand, regardless of the rules and there is – I would not say unlimited supply but there is some supply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will always be arbitraging opportunities to make money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why flats, industrial spaces, warehouses – you would have seen it in the newspapers – they even organised illegal KTV operations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if we remove the two issues, it is not that one is not connected to the other.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The pivoting of some operators is not connected to illegal activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They go on and, by definition because of our rules, if all these activities are "underground", in the sense that they are not in the open, then we have to go and use our intelligence to find and deal with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some are in these outlets; some are in outlets that are not obvious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to keep continuing at it and whatever rules we come up with, this is not going to stop.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is just a question of whether it is more or less of the activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We just have to try and deal with them.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We have completed our proceedings on the Ministerial Statements on the Fifth Update on whole-of-Government Responses to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Next is the Ministerial Statement by the Minister for Finance on Support Measures for Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Before we take the much anticipated tea break, allow me to say that the debate so far shows how we are all trying to fly our Singapore flag high throughout this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: But I thought it would be good to invite this House to show its strong support for our Team Singapore in Tokyo who are doing their best and their finest to fly our Singapore flag high at the Olympics.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And with that, I propose to take a break now.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 6.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 6.05 pm until 6.20 pm.
